title: On the floor
lead: How the Court of Master Sommeliers wants wine set up, opened, poured, decanted, stored and paired, plus the basic math behind a wine program.

intro.title: WHAT LEVEL 1 ASKS
intro.text: The Level 1 exam has basic service and food-and-wine pairing questions. In class you watch formal still and sparkling service; you are not graded on doing it. The deductive tasting method is introduced too, but it is not tested at this level (see chapter 2).

sections.name: Mise en place

lines.label: Before service
lines.text: Wine lists are clean, correct and easy to read. Glasses are spotless, free of odor, and polished with clean linen over steam.

lines.label: On the table
lines.text: Only glass stemware touches the tablecloth. Bottles, decanters and corks always sit on an underliner.

know: Glassware and service items come to the table on a tray lined with a napkin.
Serviettes are cotton or similar, so they soak up liquid, and are folded before service.
Bottles, decanters and corks go on an underliner, never straight on the tablecloth.
Wines are stored and served at the right temperature, using ice buckets or decanters when needed.
During service, serviettes are held in the hand or on the forearm, never in a pocket or on the shoulder.

visuals.title: The sommelier's kit
visuals.note: Plus pressed, clean clothes, safe shoes, clean nails and no strong perfume.

sections.name: Still wine service

lines.label: The host
lines.text: The host is the person who orders the wine. Every drink is served from the guest's right.

lines.label: The pour
lines.text: Once the host approves, pour clockwise. A guest of honor is served first. Fill glasses up to half full, depending on the glass size.

know: Take the order from the host's right and repeat it back.
Cut the foil at or below the second lip, so wine can't drip behind it. The foil goes in your pocket.
Pour the host a 1 to 1.5 oz taste, step back, and wait for approval.
Wipe the bottle after every pour, and ask before removing the cork.
A screwcap is not presented. A synthetic cork is treated like a natural cork.

items.name: Present
items.text: Label to the host; repeat the name and vintage

items.name: Cut and wipe
items.text: Foil cut below the second lip; wipe the cork top

items.name: Open
items.text: Cork out quietly; present it on an underliner, host's right

items.name: Taste
items.text: 1 to 1.5 oz for the host, then wait

items.name: Pour
items.text: Clockwise, guest of honor first; up to half full

sections.name: Sparkling wine service

lines.label: Set up
lines.text: Chill the bottle. Bring flutes or tulips, an ice bucket with stand, and two serviettes. The bucket goes to the host's right.

lines.label: Open
lines.text: Cut the foil at the bottom of the cage. Loosen the cage but leave it on. Twist the bottle, not the cork, and let the cork out quietly.

know: Never take the cage off before the cork. Keep a hand or thumb over the cage and cork the whole time.
Hold the bottle at 45 degrees, always pointed away from the guests.
Pour the host a 1 to 1.5 oz taste, just like still wine.
Fill glasses evenly, up to 3/4 full, in no more than two pours each.

items.name: HAND ON TOP
items.text: Serviette and hand over the cage and cork, always
Bottle tilted, pointed away from guests

items.name: TWIST THE BOTTLE
items.text: Not the cork. Release it quietly

items.name: 3/4 FULL
items.text: Two pours per glass, at most

sections.name: Decanting

lines.label: Why
lines.text: Old red wine is decanted to leave its sediment behind. Young Cabernet Sauvignon often benefits from decanting too.

lines.label: How
lines.text: Pour into the decanter in one smooth movement, with the bottle above a candle or flashlight. Stop when sediment reaches the shoulder.

know: Decanting is done on a gueridon (a side cart), rolled to the host's right.
Light the candle away from the table when you can.
Never look away from the bottle while decanting.
Pour the host a 1 to 1.5 oz taste from the decanter, then serve the table.

visuals.title: On the gueridon
visuals.note: Everything goes on the gueridon before it moves to the table.

sections.name: Glassware

lines.label: Placement
lines.text: Glasses go to the guest's right, keyed off the knife. Every guest's setup looks the same.

lines.label: Order
lines.text: Start with the host or the person to the host's left, then go clockwise.

know: Choose the right size and shape of glass for each wine.
Several glasses can sit in a line, diagonal, diamond or cluster, depending on table space.
A new wine's glass goes to the right of earlier glasses, so you never pour over stemware.
A second bottle of the same wine gets a fresh glass for the host's taste.
After-dinner drinks (cordials, Port, brandy) are measured with a jigger and served from the guest's right.

items.name: RIGHT SIDE
items.text: Keyed off the knife

items.name: SAME FOR ALL
items.text: Every guest's glasses match

items.name: NEW WINE
items.text: To the right of the last glass

items.name: SECOND BOTTLE

sections.name: Temperature and storage

lines.label: Serving
lines.text: The Court sets temperature ranges for its exams. They are guidelines: the wine style and the guest decide in the end.

lines.label: Storage
lines.text: Cellar wine at a constant 50-60°F (10-15°C). Keep it away from light, vibration, damp, heat, odors and pests.

know: Sparkling, light-bodied whites and sweet whites are served coldest: 42-50°F.
Full-bodied reds are served warmest: 58-65°F.
Cork-finished wines are stored on their side; spirits and fortified wines stand up.
Don't store wine upright for more than a few weeks.

visuals.title: Serving temperature · °F
visuals.note: The Court's exam guidelines. Level 1 does not ask you to memorize them.

visuals.title: Long-term storage
visuals.text: Keep it constant. The Court calls 50-60°F (10-15°C) ideal for cellaring wine.

sections.name: Hospitality and the guest

lines.label: Attitude
lines.text: The Court wants a sommelier who is quietly confident, never arrogant. No job on the floor is beneath you, and every guest should feel welcome, drinking or not.

lines.label: At the table
lines.text: Present the wine list and offer help. Be ready to recommend and to answer questions on vintage, style, food and quality.

know: If you don't know an answer, never make it up: offer to find out as soon as possible.
Discreetly find out if the host has a budget. If not, offer several wines at different prices.
When in doubt, undersell.
If a guest rejects a wine, apologize and remove it, then check it away from the table: flawed gets another bottle of the same wine; sound gets the wine list.
Never put the guest in the position of being wrong.

items.name: Acknowledge
items.text: Recognize there is a problem

items.name: Listen
items.text: Let the guest talk; listen fully

items.name: Ask
items.text: “How can I make this right?”

items.name: Decide
items.text: Based on the guest and house policy

items.name: Get help
items.text: Bring in other staff when it fits

sections.name: Food and wine pairing

lines.label: At Level 1
lines.text: The Court teaches the basic principles of food and wine pairing and the classic pairings. Both show up on the Level 1 exam.

lines.label: The main idea
lines.text: Match the wine's weight to the food. Full-bodied wines suit rich, intense dishes. Intense flavors can be too much for very delicate dishes.

know: Bold red wines go with beef and lamb.
Rich sweet wines go with dessert and foie gras.
High-acid, unoaked wines go with seafood, starters and salads.
Sancerre is a classic pairing with fresh goat cheese.
With dessert, the wine should be sweeter than the dish.

sections.name: Business of the sommelier

lines.label: At Level 1
lines.text: The Court introduces the business side at Level 1 but does not test it. It is tested at the Certified level.

lines.label: The math
lines.text: Cost of goods sold (COGS) = beginning inventory + purchases - ending inventory. Cost % = COGS ÷ wine sales.

know: A 30% wine cost means $30 in product for every $100 the business earns.
Inventory is counted in dollars: last month's count is the beginning inventory, this month's is the ending inventory.
Pours per bottle depend on pour size: divide the ounces in the bottle by the ounces per pour.
A standard bottle is 750 ml, or 25.4 oz.
The job has a front of house (guests, service, leading the team) and a back of house (vendors, buying, storing and counting the wine).

visuals.title: Bottle sizes
visuals.note: Pours per bottle = ounces in the bottle ÷ ounces per pour.

mixups.why: Still: up to half full, depending on the glass. Sparkling: up to 3/4 full, in no more than two pours.
A cork is presented on an underliner to the host's right. A screwcap goes in your pocket and is not presented.
Cork-finished table wine lies on its side. Spirits and fortified wines stand up.
COGS is dollars: (beginning inventory + purchases) - ending inventory. Cost % is COGS divided by wine sales.

facts.fact: CMS-A Hospitality & Service Standards are the basis for measuring candidates in CMS-A exams; they are formal and 'not appropriate for many restaurants'.

Required sommelier tools: 2 wine bottle openers, 2 pens, 1 pad of paper, 2 odorless lighters or matches. Appearance: pressed, cleaned attire with comfortable, safe shoes; clean fingernails; no excessive perfumes or odors.

Mise en place: wine lists clean, correct, current and easy to read; glassware clean, spotless, free of odor, polished with clean linen using steam; serviettes cotton or similar that do not repel water, folded before service; underliners, trays, ice buckets, stands and decanters clean and ready.
Glass stemware is the only thing to touch the tablecloth; bottles, decanters and corks are placed on an underliner. Glassware and service items are brought on a tray lined with a napkin.
Wines are stored and served at the correct temperature; methods include ice buckets and decanters.
Beverage service is always performed on the right side of the guest. The order is taken from the host's right and repeated. The host is the person who orders the wine.

Present the bottle and repeat name and vintage. Cut the foil at the second or lower lip to prevent wine dripping behind the foil. Wipe the cork top. Remove the cork with minimal movement and as quietly as possible. Wipe the bottle top; present the cork to the right of the host on an underliner.

Pour the host a 1-1.5 ounce taste, label facing the host; step back and wait for approval. Then serve clockwise; a guest of honor is served first; regardless of gender. Wipe the bottle after each pour. Ask to remove the cork.
Glassware placement starts with the host or the person to the host's left and continues clockwise.

Glassware: right size and shape for each wine; placed to the guest's right, keyed off the knife; line, diagonal, diamond or cluster depending on space; consistent for all guests; second bottle of the same wine gets a fresh glass for the host's taste; new wine glasses go to the right of previous glasses so the sommelier does not pour over stemware.

Sparkling: prepare glassware (tulips or flutes), ice bucket, stand and two serviettes; bottle properly chilled; bucket to the host's right. Cut the foil at the bottom of the cage. Keep a serviette and hand or thumb over cage and cork; never remove the cage; point the bottle away from guests; twist the bottle, not the cork, at 45 degrees; release as quietly as possible; remove the cage from the cork afterwards.
Sparkling: pour a 1-1.5 ounce taste; fill glasses evenly up to 3/4 full, one glass at a time, maximum two pours per glass.
White and young red wine: glasses filled up to 1/2 full depending on the size of the stemware.

Decanting items: clean decanter, matches or odorless lighter, three serviettes, three underliners for the cork, bottle and decanter, candle or small flashlight, cork removal tools, decanting basket. A gueridon is used; all materials placed on it before moving tableside; roll it to the table, preferably to the host's right. Light the candle away from the table whenever possible.

Decanting: pour slowly into the decanter in one smooth movement, bottle a safe distance above the flame; use the candle or flashlight to look for sediment at the shoulder; never look away from the bottle; stop when sediment reaches the shoulder. Pour the host a 1-1.5 ounce taste from the decanter, then serve guests.

Storage: constant temperature; 50-60°F / 10-15°C ideal for long-term storage; away from odors and pests; cork-finished table wines on their side; spirits and fortified wines standing up; avoid direct light, vibration, overly damp conditions, storing upright for over a few weeks, excessive heat or temperature swings.
Screwcap: removed quietly and placed in the sommelier's pocket; not presented. Synthetic corks are treated the same as natural corks.

Suggested serving temperatures are guidelines; wine styles and consumer preference ultimately dictate. Exam standards: Champagne and sparkling 42-50°F; light-bodied white 42-50°F; sweet white 42-50°F; dry rosé 45-55°F; full-bodied white 50-59°F; light-bodied red 50-59°F; medium-bodied red 55-62°F; full-bodied red 58-65°F.
Learning objectives include an introduction to service by observing formal still and sparkling service by the bottle, and the basic principles of food and beverage pairing.

Sommelier Skills: Deductive Tasting Method intro and Business of the Sommelier intro are 'Not tested at this level'; Food and Beverage Pairing has a section quiz; Hospitality and Service uses the Service Standards in the workbook.
Exam content includes wine and food pairing (principles and interactions; classic pairings) and basic beverage service questions. 'No need to memorize service temperatures at this time.'
Practice exam question 38: classic pairing with fresh goat cheese; options Barolo, 10-Year Tawny Port, Sancerre, Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon; answer key: C (Sancerre).
Curriculum guide, Bordeaux, Introductory column: bold red wines with beef and lamb, rich sweet wines with dessert and foie gras.

Curriculum guide, California North Coast, Introductory column: young Cabernet Sauvignon often benefits from decanting; old Cabernet Sauvignon needs decanting for sediment; match full-bodied wines with food richness and intensity.
Curriculum guide, New Zealand, Introductory column: high-acid and unoaked wines with seafood, starters, salads; intense flavors can be too much for super delicate dishes.
Curriculum guide, Champagne, Certified column: Champagne is an incredibly versatile beverage that goes with many types of foods.
Curriculum guide, Piedmont, Certified column: big tannins require meat or fat.
Curriculum guide, Sweet Wines, Certified column: match the weight of the dessert and the wine; the wine should be sweeter than the dessert.
Curriculum guide, Hungary: Tokaji bottles are normally 500ml (17oz).

Business of the Sommelier is tested in the Certified theory exam. A 30% wine cost means for every $100 of revenue, $30 is product cost. Bottle sizes: half bottle 12.7 oz / 375 ml; standard 25.4 oz / 750 ml; magnum 50.7 oz / 1500 ml / 1.5 L. Understand how pour size relates to servings per bottle. COGS = (BI + P) - EI, with BI last month's inventory and EI this month's inventory in dollars. Cost % = COGS ÷ wine sales.

Service Standards intro: mastery of beverage service combines theoretical knowledge, a trained palate, universal vocabulary, gracious carriage, respectful salesmanship and sound service mechanics. The mechanics are the foundation for world-class hospitality; reading the table's needs, understanding guest expectations and using sound sales strategies to provide a memorable dining experience remains the ultimate goal.

Standard service: the wine list is presented and assistance is offered; the sommelier is prepared to offer active and appropriate recommendations (sales skills are essential) and to answer questions on vintages, style, character of wine, food compatibility and quality. Serviettes are held in hand or on the forearm during all service and are NEVER placed in pockets or on the shoulder. The foil is placed in the sommelier's pocket.

After-dinner drinks (cordial, Port and brandy service): a gueridon or tray is used; items include measuring jiggers, a lined service tray, beverage selections, glassware and three serviettes; offer assistance and recommendations, including pairings with desserts and cheeses; measure the proper amount with a jigger; present from the guest's right.

Purchasing older wines: inquire about provenance (history of ownership), how the bottles were stored, when the bottle left the winery's cellar and how many times it has been sold or shipped; inspect for label damage, leakage and ullage.

Demeanor of the Professional Sommelier, page 1. Attitude: quietly confident but not arrogant; superlative hospitality; no job or task on the floor is beneath a sommelier; hospitality first, making guests feel welcome and comfortable whether they are drinking or not; the sommelier is part of a team. Vendors (distributors, importers, brokers and winemakers) are treated respectfully and responsibly; the supplier is part of the team. Colleagues: integrate into the service team; the sommelier is a service leader who sets the tone. Team education: share knowledge with an inclusive spirit; avoid intimidating guests or co-workers with esoteric wine information. Tableside: smile; attention always on the guest, never drawn to the sommelier; respond to compliments with brief thanks. Rapport: understand guests' priorities, wants and needs; read their response and body language. General: know the beverage program, food menu and policies; give brief, accurate descriptors without overwhelming the guest.

Demeanor of the Professional Sommelier, page 2. Do not make things up: if you do not know the answer, offer to get it as soon as possible. Discreetly determine if the host has a budget; if not, offer several selections at different price points. When in doubt, undersell. Learn and remember guests' preferences. Problem resolution: recognize and acknowledge the problem; engage the guest and let them express themselves; listen actively; ask how the issue can be addressed ('How can I make this right?'); decide what can be done based on the guest's expectation and the establishment's policies; rely on other key staff when appropriate. Rejected wine: apologize and remove the glassware and bottle; away from the table determine its condition; if flawed, offer another bottle of the same wine; if sound, offer the wine list; never put the guest in the position of being wrong. Spills: apologize, act immediately, assure the guest the restaurant will pay for dry cleaning, reseat if possible. Wrong bottle or price on a check: bring in upper management. Pricing complaints: acknowledge and tactfully state the restaurant's policies.

Course Section 12 Sommelier Skills: Introduction to the Deductive Tasting Method (workbook; not tested at this level); Food and Beverage Pairing (Curriculum Guide, workbook, section quiz); Introduction to the Business of the Sommelier (Curriculum Guide, workbook; not tested at this level); Hospitality and Service (Service Standards in workbook).
A student will NOT be tested on: wine tasting; performance of service elements; vintage memorization.

Business of the Sommelier, Introductory outcome: 'After studying this section, a student will understand basics of what the sommelier profession entails in both the back and front of the house aspects.' Introductory column (text position checked Nov 2 2026): ounces and amounts for regular sized bottles - the capacity in metric and standard for common bottle sizes: 375ml, 750ml, 1.5 liter - Magnum. Every other row (pour sizes, terms, case sizes, costing) is in the Certified column.

Intro-column pairing rows in the Curriculum Guide (text position checked Nov 2 2026): Bordeaux (bold reds with beef and lamb; rich sweet wines with dessert and foie gras), Alsace (a wide range of pairings with its diversity of wine styles), California North Coast (match full-bodied wines with food richness and intensity), New Zealand (high-acid, unoaked wines with seafood, starters, salads; intense flavors can be too much for super delicate dishes). All other regional pairing rows are in the Certified column.

unverified: Resolved Nov 2, 2026: by text position in the Curriculum Guide PDF, 'big tannins require meat or fat' (Piedmont), 'the wine should be sweeter than the dessert' (Sweet Wines) and 'Champagne goes with many types of food' sit in the Certified column. They are kept as rules of thumb. The Court's Level 1 pairing chapter is in the Introductory workbook, which is only given to enrolled students and was not checked.

Standard by-the-glass pour for still wine: the Court gives no standard size. Its costing example uses 5 pours per bottle; the curriculum guide gives 2 oz for sweet and fortified wine by the glass (and lists 2 oz as both 59.1 ml and 51.9 ml). Not used in this chapter.
The magnum card's '3 liters (101.4 oz)' is a wrong-answer option only; the Court lists no bottle larger than a magnum.
Page 1 of the Court's Demeanor of the Professional Sommelier PDF is a scanned image; it was read visually, not as extracted text.

video.title: How to Open A Bottle of Wine

keyPoints.line: is the only thing that touches the tablecloth.

2 openers, 2 pens, a pad and 2 odorless lighters.

read.bigIdea: Get everything ready before the first guest.
read.where:
The Court measures exam candidates against its **Hospitality & Service Standards**. The Court says they are formal and not right for many restaurants, but they are the exam’s yardstick.

Service starts with **mise en place**: clean lists, clean glasses and every service item ready.

stops.name: Wine lists
stops.text: Clean, correct, current and easy to read.

stops.name: Glassware
stops.text: Clean, spotless and free of odor, **polished with clean linen using steam**.

stops.name: Serviettes
stops.text: Cotton or similar, so they soak up liquid instead of repelling it. Folded before service. During service, hold them in your hand or on your forearm, **never in a pocket or on your shoulder**.

stops.name: Service items
stops.text: **Underliners**, trays, ice buckets, stands and decanters are clean and ready. Wines are stored and served at the right temperature, using ice buckets or decanters.

read.visualIntro: What the Court says every sommelier carries:
read.mixup: Only **glass stemware** touches the tablecloth. Bottles, decanters and corks always sit on an **underliner**.

video.title: How to Open A Bottle of Wine

keyPoints.line: side of the guest is where every drink is served.

read.bigIdea: Present, open, taste, then pour clockwise.
read.where: Every drink is served from the **guest’s right**. The **host** is the person who orders the wine. Take the order from the host’s right and repeat it back.

stops.name: Present
stops.text: Show the bottle to the host and repeat the **name and vintage**.

stops.name: Cut and open
stops.text: Cut the foil at or below the **second lip**, so wine can’t drip behind it, and put the foil in your pocket. Wipe the cork top, then pull the cork as quietly as you can, with little movement.

stops.name: Show the cork
stops.text: Wipe the bottle top. Present the cork on an **underliner**, to the right of the host.

stops.name: Taste
stops.text: Pour the host a **1 to 1.5 oz** taste, label facing the host. Step back and wait for approval.

stops.name: Pour
stops.text: Serve **clockwise**, guest of honor first. Fill glasses **up to half full**, depending on the glass. Wipe the bottle after every pour, and ask before removing the cork.

read.mixup: A **cork** is presented on an underliner. A **screwcap** goes in your pocket and is not presented. A synthetic cork is treated like a natural cork.
read.sayIt: Here’s the wine you ordered. May I pour you a taste?

video.title: How to Open & Serve Sparkling Wine

keyPoints.line: of the cage and cork, with a serviette, the whole time.

read.bigIdea: Keep a hand on the cork. Twist the bottle.
read.where: The Court’s steps keep a hand on the cork from start to finish. Prepare everything before you go to the table.

stops.name: Set up
stops.text: A properly **chilled** bottle, **flutes or tulips**, an ice bucket with stand and **two serviettes**. The bucket goes to the host’s right.

stops.name: Open
stops.text: Cut the foil at the **bottom of the cage**. Keep a serviette and your hand over the cage and cork. Hold the bottle at **45 degrees**, pointed away from guests, and **twist the bottle, not the cork**. Release it as quietly as you can.

stops.name: Taste
stops.text: Pour the host a **1 to 1.5 oz** taste, just like still wine.

stops.name: Pour
stops.text: Fill glasses evenly, one at a time, **up to 3/4 full**, in no more than **two pours** each.

read.mixup: **Still wine**: up to half full, depending on the glass. **Sparkling**: up to 3/4 full, in no more than two pours.

keyPoints.line: are decanted to leave the sediment behind.

read.bigIdea: Decant an old red to leave the sediment behind.
read.where:
Old Cabernet Sauvignon needs decanting for **sediment**. Young Cabernet Sauvignon often benefits from decanting too.

The Court uses a **gueridon**: everything goes on it first, then you roll it to the table, preferably to the host’s right.

stops.name: Set up
stops.text: A clean **decanter**, a **candle or small flashlight**, matches or an odorless lighter, **three serviettes**, **three underliners** (cork, bottle, decanter), cork tools and a decanting basket.

stops.name: Light
stops.text: Light the candle **away from the table** whenever you can.

stops.name: Pour
stops.text: Pour slowly in **one smooth movement**, the bottle a safe distance above the flame. Watch the **shoulder** for sediment, never look away, and stop when it reaches the shoulder.

stops.name: Serve
stops.text: Pour the host a **1 to 1.5 oz** taste from the decanter, then serve the table.

read.visualIntro: Two reasons to decant a Cabernet:
read.sayIt: This wine has some sediment, so I’ll decant it for you.

video.title: Every Wine Glass Explained By A Sommelier | World of Wine | Bon Appétit

read.bigIdea: Glasses go on the right, the same for everyone.
read.where:
Choose the **right size and shape** of glass for each wine. Place it to the guest’s right, **keyed off the knife**, and keep every guest’s setup the same.

Start with the **host** or the person to the host’s left, then go **clockwise**.

stops.name: Several glasses
stops.text: Set them in a **line, diagonal, diamond or cluster**, depending on the space on the table.

stops.name: A new wine
stops.text: Its glass goes **to the right** of the earlier glasses, so you never pour over stemware.

stops.name: A second bottle
stops.text: The host gets a **fresh glass** for the taste.

stops.name: After-dinner drinks
stops.text: Bring them on a **gueridon** or a lined tray. Measure the pour with a **jigger** and serve from the guest’s right.

read.bigIdea: Store it steady. Serve it at the right chill.
read.where: The Court sets serving temperature ranges for its exams. They are **guidelines**: the wine style and the guest decide in the end. Level 1 does not ask you to memorize them.

stops.name: Temperature
stops.text: Keep it **constant**. The Court calls **50-60°F (10-15°C)** ideal for long-term storage.

stops.name: Position
stops.text: Cork-finished table wines lie **on their side**. Spirits and fortified wines **stand up**. Don’t store wine upright for more than a few weeks.

stops.name: Keep it away from
stops.text: Direct light, vibration, damp, heat, temperature swings, odors and pests.

read.visualIntro: The Court’s exam ranges, coldest to warmest:
read.mixup: Cork-finished wine is stored **on its side**. Spirits and fortified wines are stored **standing up**.

video.title: Hospitality & Service: Court of Master Sommeliers, Americas

keyPoints.line: never arrogant. No job on the floor is beneath you.
gets the attention, never the sommelier.
offer to find the answer as soon as you can.

read.bigIdea: Take care of the guest first, every time.
read.where:
The Court’s **Service Standards** are the mechanics. The goal is a memorable meal: read the table, understand what guests expect, and sell with respect.

The Court wants a **quietly confident**, never arrogant sommelier. No job on the floor is beneath you, and every guest should feel welcome, drinking or not.

stops.name: At the table
stops.text: **Smile**, and keep the attention on the guest. Present the wine list and offer help. Give short, accurate descriptions without burying the guest in detail.

stops.name: Recommending
stops.text: Discreetly find out if the host has a **budget**. If not, offer several wines at different price points. **When in doubt, undersell.** Learn and remember what guests like.

stops.name: Not sure?
stops.text: **Never make things up.** Offer to find the answer as soon as possible.

stops.name: Something goes wrong
stops.text: Acknowledge it, let the guest talk and listen. Ask **“How can I make this right?”**, then decide based on the guest and house policy. Bring in other staff when it helps.

read.visualIntro: The Court’s fixes for four common problems:
read.mixup: A rejected wine that is **flawed** gets another bottle of the same wine. One that is **sound** gets the wine list. Either way, never make the guest wrong.
read.sayIt: I’m not sure, but let me find out for you.

keyPoints.line: full-bodied wines with rich, intense food.

read.bigIdea: Match the wine’s weight to the food.
read.where:
The Level 1 exam asks about pairing **principles** and **classic pairings**.

Full-bodied wines suit rich, intense dishes. But intense flavors can be too much for very delicate dishes.

stops.name: Beef and lamb
stops.text: **Bold red wines**, like red Bordeaux. Big tannins need meat or fat.

stops.name: Seafood, starters, salads
stops.text: **High-acid, unoaked** wines.

stops.name: Fresh goat cheese
stops.text: **Sancerre** is the classic match.

stops.name: Dessert and foie gras
stops.text: **Rich sweet wines**. With dessert, match the weight, and the wine should be **sweeter** than the dish.

read.sayIt: With the lamb, I’d suggest a bold red.

read.bigIdea: The math behind a wine program.
read.where: The Court introduces the business side at Level 1 but **does not test it**. It is tested at the **Certified** level. At Level 1 the Court wants you to know what the job involves, front and back of house, and the common bottle sizes.

stops.name: Front and back of house
stops.text: Out front, the sommelier looks after guests and leads the service team. In the back, they work with **vendors** (distributors, importers, brokers and winemakers), store the wine correctly and count inventory. When buying older wines, ask about **provenance**: who has owned it and how it was stored.

stops.name: Inventory
stops.text: Last month’s count is the **beginning inventory (BI)**. This month’s count is the **ending inventory (EI)**.

stops.name: COGS
stops.text: **COGS = (BI + purchases) − EI.** It is what the wine you sold cost you.

stops.name: Cost %
stops.text: **Cost % = COGS ÷ wine sales.** A **30%** wine cost means $30 of product for every $100 of revenue.

stops.name: Pours per bottle
stops.text: Pour size decides how many servings a bottle gives: divide the ounces in the bottle by the ounces per pour. A standard **750 ml** bottle holds **25.4 oz**.

read.mixup: **COGS** is dollars. **Cost %** is COGS divided by wine sales.
